doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Visitors at the Hickory House: Oscar Pettiford, Wilbur Ware and Monk
summary: Oscar Pettiford taught her his tunes, Wilbur Ware came in poor shape, and Monk came after she invited him, listened silently and left her the check.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Oh sure . . . just quickly give us a list of some other personalities. I remember once you told me Oscar Pettiford came by.

Oh, Pettiford. He used to . . . Oscar Pettiford came a lot, and he would sit. That’s where I learned so many of his tunes, like “Bohemia After Dark” and “Black- Eyed Peas” and . . . what was the rest of that one?
Yeah, “Blues in the Closet.”

“Swinging ’Til the Girls Come Home.” We used to play all those tunes with him. Another guy who would come in, but he would come in in not terribly good shape, Wilbur Ware. What a fine bass player he was.
Yeah. Great.
Just a tragedy.
One of the most swinging of bassists. Yeah, Wilbur. I used to call him Wilbur B. Ware. [laughs]
Yeah, right. And then Monk came in.
Did Thelonious sit in and play ever?
No.
He just visited.

It was interesting what happened with him. This is a silly anecdote. I met Monk on the street. At that time he was more communicative than in later years. He could say “hello” or something, without too much trouble. We stopped and spoke to each other, and I said, “Gee, I’m at the Hickory House. I’m so enjoying playing some of your tunes. I’m trying to learn your tunes. I’d love it if you’d come by some night.” A dumb thing, to invite Monk to hear me play his music. Anyway, he came one night. The tall, thin guy looking sinister. He had on a black raincoat and a beret, and he had a friend with him who was just as tall and sinister looking. The two of them came in, walked to the

back of the room, and sat down, ordered some drinks. I kept looking to see if there was any reaction. They were just in earnest conversation the entire set, talking back and forth. Then they got up and left, and Monk left me the check. [laughter]
He wanted to make sure that you remembered that he came [laughs], that he showed up.
Yeah, that was his comment on my rendition of “’Round Midnight,” probably. [laughter] But I think that’s so funny.
Oh I love it.

It’s wonderful. But that’s typical Monk, isn’t it? I used to go to the Five Spot a lot and hear him. He would really get up and do a little dance around the piano, a little shuffle or something, wearing one of his ridiculous hats. I went there a lot and heard him.
Probably that’s where Wilbur Ware was playing with him at some of that time.
I can’t remember. I know Wilbur Ware would do crazy things, like play on a street corner.
Yeah, Roy Haynes, maybe Johnny Griffin were in the band at that time.
It’s funny. Somehow Johnny . . .
